slides.title: Four Types of Delay in a Network
slides.body:
Why Every Packet Takes Time?
When a packet travels from a source to a destination, it does not arrive instantly. Several factors slow it down at every step. Understanding these delays helps diagnose network problems and design better systems

slides.title: Caching
slides.body:
What Does Cache Reduce?
Caching is the technique of storing a copy of frequently accessed data at a location closer to the requester, so the same data does not have to be fetched from the original source every time
Caching reduces:

slides.title: Caching Layers
slides.body:
1. DNS Cache
DNS cache stores recently resolved domain names and IP addresses
DNS records have a TTL (Time to Live), which decides how long the cached result is valid

Browser cache Stores recent DNS lookups

slides.title: CDNs
slides.body: CDNs

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
What is a CDN?
A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a group of servers placed across different locations
These servers are called edge servers or PoPs
They store cached copies of content closer to users

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
What is a CDN?
Without CDN
A user in Chennai requesting content from a US server may face high latency
During high traffic, many users hit the same origin server
This can slow down the website or overload the server

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
What is a CDN?
With CDN
Users are connected to a nearby or optimal edge server
Cached content is served faster from the edge server
The origin server handles fewer requests

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
How CDN Works?
User requests a website or content
DNS/CDN routing sends the user to a nearby edge server
The browser connects to the edge server
Cache hit: CDN serves the content directly
Cache miss: CDN fetches content from the origin, stores it, and serves it

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
What CDNs Usually Cache?
Usually Not Cached
User account data
Cart details
Cached Content
Images, videos, audio
CSS and JavaScript files
Live scores / stock prices
Static HTML pages
Personalized recommendations
Fonts and icons
Authenticated API responses
Software downloads

slides.title: Content Delivery Networks
slides.body:
Benefits of CDN
Improves availability
Helps absorb DDoS traffic
Can handle SSL/TLS at the edge server
CDN Providers

Smarter - reads the HTTP request. Can route /api/* to API servers and /images/* to image servers. Essential for microservices architectures
Types of Load Balancers

slides.title: Load Balancers - Distributing Traffic Across Multiple Servers
slides.body:
Round Robin
Load Balancing Algorithms
Sends requests one by one to each server
Example: Server 1 → Server 2 → Server 3 → Server 1
Works well when all servers have similar capacity
Limitation: It does not check current server load

slides.title: Load Balancers - Distributing Traffic Across Multiple Servers
slides.body:
Weighted Round Robin
Load Balancing Algorithms
Sends more requests to servers with higher capacity
Example: Server A with weight 3 gets more traffic than Server B with weight 1
Useful when servers have different hardware capacities

slides.title: Load Balancers - Distributing Traffic Across Multiple Servers
slides.body:
Load Balancing Algorithms
Least Connections
Sends the request to the server with the fewest active connections
Useful for long-running requests like uploads or streaming
Better than Round Robin when request duration varies

slides.title: Load Balancers - Distributing Traffic Across Multiple Servers
slides.body:
IP Hash
Uses the client’s IP address to send the same user to the same server
Helps maintain sticky sessions
Limitation: If a server fails, users may need to be remapped
Load Balancing Algorithms

slides.title: Load Balancers - Distributing Traffic Across Multiple Servers
slides.body:
Least Response Time
Sends requests to the server with the fastest response and fewer active connections
Useful for performance-sensitive applications
Limitation: Needs continuous monitoring of server response time
Load Balancing Algorithms

slides.body: End-to-End Network Design

slides.title: End-to-End
slides.body:
From Browser to Server and Back
When a user types www.amazon.in, the request passes through multiple network components before the homepage is displayed

slides.title: End-to-End - From Browser to Server and Back
slides.body:
DNS Resolution
Browser checks cache first
If not found, DNS resolver finds the IP address
DNS/CDN routing directs the user to a nearby or optimal CDN edge server
Step-by-Step Flow
1
TCP Connection
Browser creates a TCP connection with the CDN edge server
TCP uses the 3-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
2

slides.title: End-to-End - From Browser to Server and Back
slides.body:
TLS Handshake
TLS runs on top of TCP to create a secure HTTPS connection
Browser verifies the certificate
           Session keys are created for encrypted communication
3
HTTP Request
Browser sends an HTTP request, such as GET /
The request reaches the CDN edge server
4
CDN Cache Check
Cache hit: CDN serves the content directly
Cache miss: CDN forwards the request to the origin server
5
Step-by-Step Flow

slides.title: End-to-End - From Browser to Server and Back
slides.body:
Load Balancer
At the origin, the load balancer receives the request
It checks healthy backend servers
It forwards the request to a suitable server
6
Backend Processing
The backend server processes the request
It may fetch data from databases or caches like Redis
It prepares the response
7
Step-by-Step Flow

slides.title: End-to-End - From Browser to Server and Back
slides.body:
Response and Rendering
Response travels back to the browser
Browser loads HTML, CSS, JS, images, and fonts
Many static files may come from the CDN cache
The page is finally rendered
8
Step-by-Step Flow

slides.title: Scaling the Internet
slides.body:
From One Server To Millions
When traffic grows from hundreds to millions of users, a single server cannot keep up. Modern systems scale using four core strategies

slides.title: Scaling the Internet
slides.body:
From One Server To Millions
Add more CPU, RAM, or storage to a single server. Simple, but has a hard hardware ceiling and creates a single point of failure
Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)
Add more servers and distribute traffic using a load balancer. No theoretical upper limit. Requires services to be stateless - session state must live in a shared store like Redis, not on the server itself

slides.title: Scaling the Internet
slides.body:
From One Server To Millions
It automatically adds or removes servers based on demand (Eg: CPU usage, traffic), ensuring enough capacity during spikes while avoiding unnecessary resources during low traffic
Multi-Region Deployment
Run the system across multiple geographic regions. Users are routed to the nearest region for low latency. If one region fails, traffic fails over to another automatically

slides.body:
